title: My mare's swabs are clean, so why won't she get in foal?
description: A clean swab does not always mean a clean uterus. Dr. Morten Rønn Petersen explains why some infections sit in the tissue where a swab cannot find them.
transcript: We get the question a lot: why are my mare's swabs clean, but she doesn't get in foal? It has a lot to do with two things. It has to do with the type of diagnostic tool you use. Is it a swab, a lavage of the uterus, or a biopsy? It's known that you can miss infections if you only use a swab. The swab is fast and easy to use, but will only pick up the superficial infections that are evenly distributed throughout the uterus. Some bacteria can establish an infection within the tissue, and that's the case with the streptococci. When the bacteria are not metabolically active and they sit within the tissue, they cannot be picked up with the swab, sometimes not even with the biopsy. The main thing is that they are metabolically inactive, and that's why they need to be activated to be detected with the diagnostic test. So we're using the right tool to diagnose, and then activate the bacteria. That's the trick.

title: What can I do about a problem mare that won't get pregnant?
description: Normal cycles, good semen, bred at the right time, and still empty. Dr. Morten Rønn Petersen on what to look for next.
transcript: We often get the question: what can I do about a problem mare that won't get pregnant? There are a lot of things that can affect why a mare doesn't get pregnant. But in problem mares, we expect that the semen is fertile, the mare is bred at the right time, and the mare has been checked for uterine infections. In these problem mares, there's a very high risk that the mare is chronically infected with dormant bacteria sitting within the uterine tissue. The only way to identify these bacteria is to activate them so that they become metabolically active. They come to the surface of the uterus, and then you can identify them. And when they are metabolically active, they also become sensitive to antibiotics, and then you can treat the mare effectively.

title: How do you find a hidden uterine infection in a mare?
description: How activation culture works, step by step, explained by Dr. Morten Rønn Petersen, who developed the method.
transcript: How do you find a hidden uterine infection in a mare? These hidden uterine infections are a common scenario in problem mares. The key is to activate the bacteria hiding within the uterus so that they become metabolically active. They come to the surface of the uterus, and then you can identify them and treat them. That is done using bActivate and the regular techniques the vet is using. You do a uterine culture. We recommend a low-volume lavage, and right after that you deposit bActivate in the uterus of the mare. Then you come back two days later and repeat the uterine sampling. When you have the culture results from the sample before activation and two days after activation, you can see whether bacteria have been activated. Then you treat according to the sensitivity, so that you know your treatment is effective. You treat locally and systemically with antibiotics.

title: Is my mare too old to breed, or could it be something else?
description: Age lowers fertility, but it is not the whole story. Dr. Morten Rønn Petersen on which mares are most at risk of a dormant uterine infection.
transcript: Is my mare too old to breed, or could it be something else? When a mare gets older, the chances of pregnancy are reduced, but it's not zero. The thing to keep in mind is that as her age increases, the risk of uterine infections also increases, as the mare produces foals over time. So if the mare is more than twelve years of age, if she's had three or more foals, or a history of endometritis, then we know that the risk is very high for a chronic dormant uterine infection.
